current_episode.title: E432: $24 Billion Investor on Private Credit, the Psychology of Winning & Fear of Failure

guest.bio_context: David Weisburd has a background in accounting, finance, and law, having practiced law for approximately 14 years specializing in M&A and bank financing law for private equity transactions. He founded Monaro Capital in 2001 to serve the lower middle market with creative, flexible financing solutions. Today, Monaro Capital manages $24 billion in assets and deploys approximately $10 billion annually.

context.real_quote: Don't focus on your accomplishments. Focus on the work that you've done, the effort you've put in to get there, and then keep moving your goals.

context.transcript_excerpt: Monaro Capital has grown to $24 billion firm, deploying $10 billion a year. But when you started in 2001, it was a completely different market. What made you want to enter private credit? Excellent question. So my background is accounting and finance and law. I practiced law for about 14 years. I did M&A and bank financing law, mostly for private equity transactions. And what I noticed is that throughout my career, we worked with banks on transactions. Banks were relatively inflexible in terms of their financing because they had regulations and they had certain ways they had to do deals. The only two non-banks that existed at that time were GE Capital and Heller Financial. And they weren't regulated, so they could structure deals in all kinds of more creative ways and customize transactions for companies. They were doing larger deals. There was nobody really doing lower middle market or smaller deals in a non-bank format. So I thought that as opposed to working 24-7 and building hours as a lawyer, that I could take what I learned as a lawyer, take what I learned representing PE funds and banks and apply that to transactional finance and do it the way GE Capital and Heller Financial were doing it in a way that was more user-friendly for smaller companies, more Main Street America. And I started Monroe in 2001 and managed to recruit three guys that were excellent bankers. One was a credit guy. One was an origination person. One was an underwriter that joined me in this new venture. They were each making $100,000 a year, and they had families, and they were a little reticent to do it, but I convinced them that we were going to be successful, and this was going to be the new form of finance as the future unfolded. I'm so curious because not that much innovation is done in the financial markets. What made you so confident that you were on the cusp of a new asset class? I didn't. I just was tired and burnt out being a lawyer and I wanted to build something. I'm an entrepreneur at heart and I'm a business builder. And I thought that if I could get a clean shot at building a banking product, a finance product, the good news is banking has been around forever. Transaction finance was being done by banks. and I was confident that if I could come in and do the same type of financing, but with less rules and providing more creativity, that we could build a business. Now, at the end of the day, I didn't know how big of a business we could build. I thought we could build a business. We could put a couple hundred million dollars, three, four hundred million dollars to work, and it would be a success. So what happened is that I got into it and I realized that there was a much bigger market here than I had anticipated. And that I had to realign my thinking into how to build a business as opposed to just do deals. And your original goal was $300 million, $400 million. Today, as I mentioned, you have $24 billion deployed. What gets you up every day to keep on building the business bigger and bigger? Another good question. I think part of that is being an entrepreneur, and part of that is being afraid to fail. Every day I get up and I think about how we can grow the business, what we can do, what new areas we can get into. I was always a competitive ball player. I was a basketball guy. If I didn't do this, my first goal was to be a professional basketball player. That didn't quite work out the way I wanted. so I had to default into my next goal, which was accounting and finance. So it's the competitive spirit. It's about winning. It's not about dollars. It's not about numbers. I keep telling people that the way to be successful in whatever career that you want to pursue is not by being satisfied. It's always by moving the goalposts out. Once you have an achievement, don't rest on your achievement. Don't rest on your laurels. Don't read the newspaper clippings. One of my favorite analogies is I'm a sports guy. I'm a big basketball guy. Michael Jor

pending_qa.q: What are the two primary ways to generate alpha in the private credit asset class?
pending_qa.r: The two ways to generate alpha in private credit are: one, making more money than the next guy, and two, losing less money than the next guy. Private credit is fixed income, not designed for 2x, 3x, or 5x returns; instead, it focuses on generating safe, stable, consistent returns that institutional investors like pension funds and insurance companies depend on year after year.

pending_qa.q: Why does David Weisburd focus Monaro Capital exclusively on the lower middle market rather than larger deals?
pending_qa.r: Weisburd focuses on companies with $35–$40 million EBITDA and below because Wall Street ignores this segment, preferring larger upper middle market deals. The lower middle market represents 50% of U.S. employment, consists of approximately 200,000 middle market companies, and generates one-third of U.S. GDP. By focusing on Main Street America, Monaro built the largest and best firm in that underserved niche.

pending_qa.q: How does personal and family history shape an entrepreneur's competitive drive and motivation for sustained growth?
pending_qa.r: Weisburd's father was a Holocaust survivor who was liberated from Dachau, fought in the Israeli independence war, and came to the U.S. as an immigrant, serving in Korea to earn citizenship. As the first in his family to attend college, Weisburd felt driven to achieve something his father and family never could. He consciously channels adverse experiences and family legacy as fuel to push beyond what he thinks is possible, a philosophy he shares with mentees and younger people in his organization.

pending_qa.q: What is Weisburd's core philosophy on avoiding complacency and sustaining competitive excellence?
pending_qa.r: Weisburd emphasizes moving the goalposts continuously rather than resting on achievements. He uses Michael Jordan as an example—Jordan never read newspaper clippings about his accomplishments but instead focused on daily work and performance. The key is not to focus on accomplishments but on the effort and work behind them, then keep moving goals forward, because if you stop moving them, you will never reach the next level of achievement.

pending_qa.q: How has Monaro Capital's compound growth rate compared to other industries over the 2010–2020 period?
pending_qa.r: From 2010 to 2020, Monaro Capital grew its business at approximately 25–30% per year on a compounded basis. Weisburd notes that no other industry or business has achieved that rate of growth during that period, which he attributes to having built the business model before the financial crisis and then stepping on the gas once regulators changed the rules for banks.
